rationale: B wins because it keeps its hands mostly inside the fact box; "Allbirds says its new sugarcane-and-wool shoe outlasts the original wool runner — now it has to prove it" is a clean tension a trade reporter can test. A is more muscular, but "A DTC pioneer that spent a decade avoiding wholesale" is an invented spine, and its sustainability angle drags in carbon-footprint logic the update never gave it. The winner is less flashy and less likely to embarrass the founder in the first reply.
gaps_in_A: "A DTC pioneer that spent a decade avoiding wholesale" is not in the update. If that history is wrong, the channel angle collapses before the reporter gets to paragraph two.

"That's a company publicly conceding its signature product had a durability problem" overstates the supplied fact. "More durable than the original" is not the same as an admission that the old shoe failed.
"The sustainable-shoe brand" plus "low-carbon materials" and "carbon footprint" imports a climate thesis the update did not provide. It may be true, but this exercise did not give it to you.
"the same story told in one quarter" implies a tighter timing and causal chain among closures, wholesale, and margin improvement than the facts support.
gaps_in_B: "Allbirds' comeback runs through someone else's shelves" uses the recovery narrative the facts do not support. A company that is still unprofitable and below IPO price has not earned "comeback."
"category-creation" is the wrong label for the sugarcane-and-wool durability angle. This is a materials proof story, not category creation.

"the platform is the centerpiece of the relaunch" is stronger than the update says. The facts say the platform exists and the wholesale partnership is part of the relaunch, not which one is the centerpiece.
The refused angles are good, but they fail to police the set's own spin: "comeback" should have been killed there too.
